data.description: Evaluates a template expression against local_state and routes to one of two named steps without performing any I/O. Truthy: non-empty, non-"null", non-"undefined", non-"0". on_success and on_else use bare step keys (e.g. "2", "3a") — same rule as all other routing fields. No output_key is written.

input_contract.description: {{template}} expression resolved against local_state — e.g. "{{input.id}}"
Bare step key to jump to when expression is truthy (e.g. "2", "3a")
Bare step key to jump to when expression is falsy (e.g. "3", "4b")

data.description: Terminal step — marks the workflow run as completed. No input or output fields. Every workflow must have exactly one end step as its final step.

Suspends workflow execution and presents a dialog to the user. Execution resumes when the user clicks an option button. Gate types: confirm (read message, click button), edit_list (review and remove items), text_input (type free text in the input field), review_object (review key/value summary), choice (single-select with lettered buttons and per-option descriptions — output_key written with selected value; if button has modal descriptor, typed modal text written to option's own output_key if declared, or step-level output_key if not). Each option has its own on_select routing token. special_buttons appear as action buttons only, never in description lists, and support modal descriptors. reveal: optional single task_card shown inline above the gate buttons — { button_label, content }. reveals: array version — one task_card per entry; supports inline array or {{template}} reference to local_state array.

input_contract.description: confirm | edit_list | text_input | review_object | choice
Message shown to user — supports {{template}} substitution
Dot-path into local_state for the data shown in the dialog (required for edit_list and review_object)

Array of option objects — must include at least one with action/value: "cancel". Shape by gate_type: confirm/edit_list/review_object use { label, action, on_select }; choice uses { value, label, description, on_select } where value is the machine identifier. Any option may carry a modal descriptor: { title, input_label, placeholder, multiline } — clicking opens an overlay modal. For choice options with a modal, also add output_key to route the modal text to a specific local_state key instead of the step-level output_key.

Optional buttons appended after options. Never appear in description_list. Use for Cancel or modal-trigger buttons. Supports modal descriptor: { title, input_label, placeholder, multiline }. Cancel obligation can be satisfied here instead of in options.
text_input only — short label above the inline text input. Defaults to "Your input".
text_input: typed value written on submit. confirm+context_key: selected action written. choice: selected option.value written — overridden by modal inputValue when button has modal descriptor.
Default routing when no on_select override applies
Routing on gate execution error — not user cancellation

Optional single task_card shown inline above the gate buttons. Shape: { button_label: string, content: string }. Does NOT advance the workflow. content supports {{template}} substitution. Use reveals (array) when the number of cards is determined at runtime.

Array version of reveal — one task_card per entry. Each entry: { button_label: string, content: string }. Supports inline array or {{template}} reference to a local_state array. Use when the number of cards is determined at runtime (e.g. one card per table).

data.description: Executes a single item_step once per element of an array in local_state. Sequential only — one item at a time. Collects results into an array at output_key. Items must be an array written by a prior step. Two categories: non-suspending (serv_*, llm_call, js_transform item steps — all items run inline in one Lambda invocation) and suspending (human_gate item step — suspends once per item, resumes on user response). Only gate_type: "choice" is valid as a suspending item_step.

input_contract.description: Dot-path into local_state resolving to the array to iterate over

Step definition executed once per item. Use {{item}} or {{item.field}} to reference the current element. All parent local_state keys are also readable. Non-suspending item_steps (serv_schema, serv_insert, serv_update, serv_delete, serv_query, llm_call, js_transform) run inline in a single Lambda invocation. Suspending item_steps (human_gate) suspend once per item and resume on user response — only gate_type: "choice" is valid inside an iterator. Dynamic options pattern: set "options": "{{item.options}}" on the human_gate item_step — the single-token template resolves to the item's options array at runtime, enabling per-item dynamic choice lists built by a prior js_transform step.
local_state key where collected results array is written after all items complete
Routing token after all items complete — defaults to "next"
Must always be "sequential". Omitting this field is a workflow defect.
Routing token if an item_step fails

output_contract.description: Array of outputValue from each item_step execution

data.description: Runs a pure synchronous JS expression via acorn AST gate + vm.runInNewContext(200ms). Two bindings available: (1) items — the resolved value of input_key from local_state. (2) local_state — the full workflow state object; use local_state.key_name to read any prior step output across steps. No async, no I/O, no Node globals. Expression must be an IIFE or value expression that returns the output. Use for score tallies, filters, aggregations, string formatting, loop state mutations.

input_contract.description: Synchronous JS IIFE or value expression. items = resolved input_key value. local_state = full workflow state. Must return the output value. Example: (function(){ return items.filter(r => r.score > 0).length; })()
Dot-path into local_state resolving to the input value bound as 'items'. Required.
Dot-path where the result is written to local_state
Routing token — supports step:N for backward loops

output_contract.description: Result of the expression written to local_state[output_key]

data.description: Calls an LLM using a named prompt from PGC_Prompt. Resolves template variables from local_state into the prompt. Runs the 2-attempt validation/correction loop. Writes the validated output object to output_key.

input_contract.description: intent_category key into PGC_Prompt — identifies which prompt to use
local_state key where the validated LLM output object is written

Additional keys in input (beyond prompt) become {{key}} substitution variables in the prompt text. Key name must match the placeholder exactly — snake_case user_input matches {{user_input}}, NOT {{userInput}}. user_input is also sent as the LLM human/user message.
Routing token — defaults to "next"
Routing token — use "cancel" for unrecoverable failures

output_contract.description: The validated LLM output object written to local_state[output_key]

data.description: Sends a message to the user via the callback channel. The message_template is resolved against local_state. Does not block — fire and forget. Typically the second-to-last step before "end".

input_contract.description: Message text — supports {{template}} substitution from local_state
SQS message type — defaults to HUMAN_NOTIFICATION
Routing token — typically "end" on the final notify step

sections.data:
ROUTING VALUE RULES — every on_success, on_else, on_cancel, and on_select field in a workflow step must use one of these exact tokens:

  next        — advance to the sequentially next step in the array
  end         — terminate the workflow run as completed
  cancel      — cancel the run and clear the stack (same effect as the user clicking Cancel)
  <key>       — a bare step key string — jump directly to the step whose "step" field matches (e.g. "3", "3a", "12b")

NOTES:
- Use the actual step key string as-is: "3a" jumps to the step whose "step" field is "3a". No prefix required.
- Backward references (routing to an earlier step key) are safe ONLY when there is at least one human_gate on the path from the target back to the source. Without a gate, backward references create infinite loops.
- on_else should be "cancel" for any step that calls an external service (llm_call, serv_query, serv_insert, serv_update, serv_delete) and fails unrecoverably.
- Every human_gate MUST have at least one option with action: "cancel". This is enforced by the static analysis validator.
- notify steps only support "next" and "end" in on_success — they have no on_else.
- end steps have no routing fields.
- condition on_success and on_else also use bare step keys (the same rule applies to all routing fields).

COMMON MISTAKE — step: prefix:
  WRONG:  "on_success": "step:8"  (step: prefix is not needed)
  RIGHT:  "on_success": "8"       (bare step key)

WORKED EXAMPLE — create_domain workflow (condensed data flow)

This is the canonical example of a correct workflow definition. Use it as the reference for step structure, template syntax, data flow, and the expression-based js_transform pattern.

run.input = { userInput: "stock portfolio" }

Step 1  llm_call (prompt: "create_domain", user_input: "{{input.userInput}}")
        → output_key: "proposed_scaffold"
        → local_state.proposed_scaffold = { domain: "stock_portfolio", tables: [...] }
        → on_success: "next", on_else: "cancel"

Step 2  js_transform (expression-based, input_key: "proposed_scaffold.tables", output_key: "proposed_scaffold.tables")
        expression: "(function() { var SYS = new Set(['id','created_at','updated_at']); return items.map(function(t) { var cols = t.columns.filter(function(c){ return !SYS.has(c.name); }).slice(0,4).map(function(c){ return c.name; }); return Object.assign({}, t, { columnSummary: cols.join(', '), domain: local_state.proposed_scaffold.domain }); }); })()"
        → enriches each table with columnSummary field
        → NOTE: local_state is a first-class sandbox binding — use local_state.key_name to read any prior step output
        → NOTE: transform_type built-ins (columnSummary, buildChildInserts, etc.) are REMOVED — always use expression
        → on_success: "next"

Step 3  human_gate (gate_type: "edit_list", context_key: "proposed_scaffold.tables")
        → options: [confirm→"step:3d", add_table→"step:3a", cancel→"cancel"]
        → on_success: "next", on_else: "cancel"

Step 3a human_gate (gate_type: "text_input", output_key: "new_table_description")
        → user types table description, written to local_state.new_table_description
        → on_success: "next", on_else: "cancel"

Step 3b llm_call (prompt: "design_table", inputs: domain, existing_tables, user_input)
        → output_key: "new_table"

Step 3c js_transform (expression merges new_table into proposed_scaffold.tables)
        → reads local_state.new_table and local_state.proposed_scaffold via local_state binding
        → on_success: "step:3"  ← intentional backward reference (safe — step 3 is a human_gate)

Step 3d human_gate (gate_type: "review_object", context_key: "proposed_scaffold.tables")
        → confirm → "next", cancel → "cancel"

Step 4  human_gate (gate_type: "confirm") — final DDL confirmation
        → confirm → "next", cancel → "cancel"

Step 5  iterator (items_key: "proposed_scaffold.tables", execution_mode: "sequential")
          item_step: serv_schema createTable({{item}})
        → output_key: "created_tables", on_complete: "next"

Step 6  js_transform (expression derives registration data from scaffold — no LLM)
        → reads: local_state.proposed_scaffold.domain, local_state.proposed_scaffold.tables
        → output_key: "generated" = { domainHelp, intentMapRows, entitySchemas }

Step 7  human_gate (gate_type: "review_object", context_key: "generated.domainHelp")
        → confirm → "next", cancel → "cancel"

Step 8  serv_insert (tableName: "PGC_DomainHelp", row: "{{generated.domainHelp}}")

Step 9  iterator over generated.intentMapRows — serv_insert PGC_IntentMap({{item}})

Step 10b iterator over generated.entitySchemas — serv_insert PGC_EntitySchema({{item}})

Step 11 notify "Domain {{proposed_scaffold.domain}} created."
        → on_success: "end"

Step 12 end

KEY PATTERNS FROM THIS EXAMPLE:
- Template syntax: {{key}}, {{key.field}}, {{key.0.field}}, {{item}}, {{item.field}}, {{input.field}}
- output_key establishes the local_state key that downstream steps reference
- js_transform ALWAYS uses expression — never transform_type (built-ins are removed)
- expression is an IIFE: (function(){ ... return value; })()
- local_state is available in every expression — read any prior step output via local_state.key_name
- Backward references (step:3) are safe only when every path back passes through at least one human_gate
- serv_insert row values use template substitution: "{{generated.domainHelp}}" resolves to the full object
- iterator must always include execution_mode: "sequential"

FLAT LOOP PATTERN — for workflows that iterate over a collection with human interaction per item:

Use this when a simple iterator cannot be used because each item requires human interaction (e.g. a quiz, a review flow, a step-by-step tutorial).

Example: item review queue
  state: local_state.items (array loaded once), local_state.index (0), local_state.tally ({ approved:0, rejected:0 })

  Step 1: serv_entity_query — load items into local_state.items
  Step 2: js_transform — initialise index=0 and tally using (function(){ return { items: items, index: 0, tally: {approved:0,rejected:0} }; })()
          output_key: "loop_state"
  Step 3: js_transform — pick current item: (function(){ return local_state.loop_state.items[local_state.loop_state.index]; })()
          input_key: "loop_state", output_key: "current_item"
  Step 4: human_gate confirm — show item details (message_template: "Item: {{current_item.name}} — {{current_item.description}}"), options: [Review→next, Cancel→cancel]
  Step 5: human_gate choice — user approves or rejects the item, output_key: "user_decision"
  Step 6: js_transform — update tally and advance index:
          expression: (function(){ var ls = local_state.loop_state; var approved = local_state.user_decision==='approve'; var t = { approved: ls.tally.approved+(approved?1:0), rejected: ls.tally.rejected+(approved?0:1) }; return { items: ls.items, index: ls.index+1, tally: t }; })()
          input_key: "loop_state", output_key: "loop_state"
  Step 7: human_gate confirm — show decision recorded (message_template: "Decision logged."), options: [Next item→step:3, Finish→step:8, Cancel→cancel]
          ← BACKWARD REFERENCE: step:3 is safe because steps 4, 5, 7 are human_gates in the loop path
  Step 8: js_transform — compute loop_done = index >= items.length, output_key: "loop_done"
  Step 9: condition — check loop_done: on_success→step:10, on_else→step:3
  Step 10: notify — review summary
  Step 11: end

FLAT LOOP GUARD 3 SAFETY RULE:
- A backward reference (e.g. step 8 → step:3) is SAFE if and only if the path from the target step back to the source step contains at least one human_gate
- Without a human_gate in the loop, the Step Processor spins synchronously and exhausts Lambda
- Always verify: target_step ... [human_gate] ... source_step ... backward_ref → target_step

STEP USAGE PATTERNS — concrete correct forms for each step type

These patterns show exactly how to write each step type. The most common mistake
for each type is noted. Use these alongside the step_type_contracts schema.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
js_transform — expression-based data manipulation
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: input_key, output_key, expression, on_success
expression MUST be a synchronous IIFE that returns the output value.

Correct — enrich an array, read cross-step state via local_state:
{
  "step": "2", "type": "js_transform",
  "input_key": "proposed_scaffold.tables",
  "output_key": "proposed_scaffold.tables",
  "expression": "(function() { return items.map(function(t) { return Object.assign({}, t, { domain: local_state.proposed_scaffold.domain }); }); })()",
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}

Correct — update a loop counter using cross-step local_state reads:
{
  "step": "7", "type": "js_transform",
  "input_key": "loop_state",
  "output_key": "loop_state",
  "expression": "(function() { var ls = local_state.loop_state; var approved = local_state.user_decision==='approve'; return { items: ls.items, index: ls.index+1, tally: { approved: ls.tally.approved+(approved?1:0), rejected: ls.tally.rejected+(approved?0:1) } }; })()",
  "on_success": "next"
}

Correct — compute a boolean flag for a condition step:
{
  "step": "8a", "type": "js_transform",
  "input_key": "loop_state",
  "output_key": "loop_done",
  "expression": "(function() { var ls = local_state.loop_state; return ls.index >= ls.items.length; })()",
  "on_success": "next"
}

MISTAKES:
✗ expression that is not an IIFE: "items.filter(...)" — must be (function(){...return ...;})()
✗ using output_key as a dot-path to merge into a parent: "loop_state.done" — only top-level keys are reliable write targets; for nested writes, return the full updated object
✗ trying to await or fetch inside expression — no async, no I/O

────────────────────────────────────────────────
condition — routes on a boolean expression, no I/O
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: expression, on_success, on_else
on_success and on_else are BARE STEP KEYS — same rule as all other routing fields.
Do NOT use "step:N" format here.

Correct:
{
  "step": "8b", "type": "condition",
  "expression": "{{loop_done}}",
  "on_success": "10",
  "on_else": "3"
}

MISTAKES:
✗ on_success: "step:3" — WRONG. Use bare key: "3"
✗ condition writes no output_key — it produces no local_state value
✗ using a {{template}} that resolves to a complex object — expression must resolve to a truthy/falsy scalar. Write a boolean flag in a prior js_transform and condition on that flag.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
human_gate — confirm type (simple acknowledgement)
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: gate_type, message_template, options (must include cancel)

Correct — simple confirmation before a destructive action:
{
  "step": "4", "type": "human_gate", "gate_type": "confirm",
  "message_template": "Delete {{input.entity_name}} id={{input.id}}? This cannot be undone.",
  "options": [
    { "label": "Confirm delete", "action": "confirm", "on_select": "next" },
    { "label": "Cancel",         "action": "cancel",  "on_select": "cancel" }
  ],
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}

Correct — confirm gate with context_key shows the data object above the buttons.
When context_key is present and output_key is set, the user's selected action
value is written to local_state[output_key]:
{
  "step": "3", "type": "human_gate", "gate_type": "confirm",
  "message_template": "What would you like help with?",
  "context_key": "help_options.domainButtons",
  "output_key": "help_selection",
  "options": [
    { "label": "System commands", "action": "system", "on_select": "next" },
    { "label": "Cancel",          "action": "cancel", "on_select": "cancel" }
  ],
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}

MISTAKES:
✗ output_key on a confirm gate WITHOUT context_key — the value is never written. output_key only writes on text_input gates and on confirm gates that also have context_key.
✗ missing cancel option — required by static analysis validator.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
human_gate — text_input type (free text capture)
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: gate_type: "text_input", message_template, output_key, options
output_key is REQUIRED and is the local_state key where the typed value is written on submit.
No context_key — text_input shows only the message_template.
Options must have exactly one Submit (action: confirm) and one Cancel.

Correct:
{
  "step": "5", "type": "human_gate", "gate_type": "text_input",
  "message_template": "{{current_item.description}}\n\nType the matching value:",
  "output_key": "user_answer",
  "options": [
    { "label": "Submit", "action": "confirm", "on_select": "next" },
    { "label": "Cancel", "action": "cancel",  "on_select": "cancel" }
  ],
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}

MISTAKES:
✗ context_key on text_input — invalid, ignored
✗ omitting output_key — the typed value is lost
✗ output_key on confirm/review_object gate types — has no effect; only text_input writes on submit

────────────────────────────────────────────────
human_gate — review_object type (structured summary)
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: gate_type: "review_object", message_template, context_key, options

Correct:
{
  "step": "3", "type": "human_gate", "gate_type": "review_object",
  "message_template": "Here's what I parsed. Does this look right?",
  "context_key": "parsed_entity",
  "options": [
    { "label": "Looks good", "action": "confirm", "on_select": "next" },
    { "label": "Cancel",     "action": "cancel",  "on_select": "cancel" }
  ],
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}

────────────────────────────────────────────────
iterator — sequential execution over an array
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: items_key, item_step, output_key, on_complete, execution_mode
execution_mode MUST always be "sequential". Without it the iterator is non-sequential
and large batches will exhaust Lambda concurrency.
item_step uses {{item}} and {{item.field}} to reference the current element.

Correct:
{
  "step": "6", "type": "iterator",
  "items_key": "child_inserts",
  "item_step": {
    "type": "serv_insert",
    "input": { "tableName": "{{item.tableName}}", "row": "{{item.row}}" },
    "on_else": "cancel"
  },
  "execution_mode": "sequential",
  "output_key": "inserted_children",
  "on_complete": "next",
  "on_else": "cancel"
}

MISTAKES:
✗ omitting execution_mode — always required
✗ item_step referencing local_state keys that do not exist yet — item_step runs with the parent frame's local_state plus the injected 'item' key
✗ output_key omitted — iterator results are lost



────────────────────────────────────────────────
human_gate — choice type (single-select with descriptions)
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: gate_type: "choice", message_template, options (value/label/description shape)
output_key is written with the selected option's value when the user responds.
Options use { value, label, description, on_select } — value is the machine identifier
written to output_key, label is the short button text, description is shown above buttons.

Correct — standalone choice gate:
{
  "step": "3b", "type": "human_gate", "gate_type": "choice",
  "message_template": "How should the workflow evaluate the response?",
  "output_key": "eval_preference",
  "options": [
    { "value": "llm",    "label": "A", "description": "LLM grades each answer — precise but uses tokens", "on_select": "next" },
    { "value": "self",   "label": "B", "description": "Self-report pass/fail after seeing the answer",     "on_select": "next" },
    { "value": "cancel", "label": "Cancel", "description": "Stop workflow",                               "on_select": "cancel" }
  ],
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}

Correct — choice gate as item_step inside a suspending iterator:
{
  "step": "5", "type": "iterator",
  "items_key": "preference_gates",
  "item_step": {
    "type": "human_gate",
    "gate_type": "choice",
    "message_template": "{{item.question}}",
    "options": "{{item.options}}",
    "output_key": "user_preferences",
    "on_success": "next",
    "on_else": "cancel"
  },
  "execution_mode": "sequential",
  "output_key": "user_preferences",
  "on_complete": "next",
  "on_else": "cancel"
}
Each item in preference_gates must have shape: { question, options: [{value, label, description, on_select}] }
The iterator suspends once per item. resume_gate increments current_index and strips
the item binding before merging state back onto the iterator frame.
The results array at output_key collects one selected value per item.


Correct — choice gate with iterator on option (one button per array item):
{
  "step": "3", "type": "human_gate", "gate_type": "choice",
  "message_template": "Select a collection:\n{{items_list}}",
  "output_key": "selected_collection_id",
  "options": [
    { "value": "{{id}}", "label": "{{name}}", "description": "{{card_count}} cards", "on_select": "next", "iterator": "decks" },
    { "value": "cancel", "label": "Cancel", "description": "Stop", "on_select": "cancel" }
  ],
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}
The iterator field on an option expands it into one button per item in localState["decks"].
Tokens in label/value/description resolve against {...localState, ...item}.
Do NOT add a preceding js_transform to build the options array — use iterator instead.
MISTAKES:
✗ Using confirm, edit_list, review_object, or text_input as item_step gate_type inside
  an iterator — only choice composes correctly into a results array per item.
✗ Omitting execution_mode: "sequential" on any iterator — always required.
✗ Using a suspending iterator when inter-item state is needed — use the flat loop
  pattern instead (backward step reference with a human_gate in the loop path).
  See the flat loop example in create_domain_example system context.

✗ Adding a js_transform step before a choice human_gate to format the options array —
  set iterator: '<local_state_key>' on the option object instead. The iterator pattern
  is handled natively by buildDialog and requires no extra step.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
llm_call — calling an existing prompt
────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED fields: input.prompt (intent_category), output_key, on_success, on_else
input.prompt must match an intent_category in PGC_Prompt. All other input keys
become {{template}} substitutions in the prompt text.

Correct:
{
  "step": "6", "type": "llm_call",
  "input": {
    "prompt": "evaluate_translation",
    "term":        "{{current_card.term}}",
    "definition":  "{{current_card.definition}}",
    "user_answer": "{{user_answer}}"
  },
  "output_key": "eval_result",
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel"
}

MISTAKES:
✗ referencing a prompt intent_category that does not exist in PGC_Prompt — check design_spec.prompts_needed to confirm the prompt was seeded
✗ adding output_schema to an llm_call step — output_schema is defined on the PGC_Prompt row, not on the step
────────────────────────────────────────────────
iterator + human_gate (choice) — dynamic preference gates
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Use this pattern when the right brain research step returns preference_questions and you
need to present each question as a separate human_gate choice to the user.

Step A — js_transform builds the preference_gates array from right_brain_research output:
{
  "step": "A", "type": "js_transform",
  "input_key": "right_brain_research",
  "output_key": "preference_gates",
  "expression": "(function() { var letters = ['A','B','C','D','E']; return (items.preference_questions || []).map(function(q) { var opts = (q.options || []).map(function(o, i) { return { value: o.value, label: letters[i] || String.fromCharCode(65+i), description: o.description || '', on_select: 'next' }; }); opts.push({ value: 'na', label: 'N/A', description: 'Not applicable to my use case', on_select: 'next' }); opts.push({ value: 'cancel', label: 'Cancel', description: '', on_select: 'cancel' }); return { id: q.id, question: q.question, options: opts }; }); })()",
  "on_success": "next"
}

Step B — condition skips iterator if no questions were found:
{
  "step": "B", "type": "condition",
  "expression": "{{preference_gates.length}}",
  "on_success": "C",
  "on_else": "D"
}

Step C — iterator presents each preference question as a choice gate:
{
  "step": "C", "type": "iterator",
  "items_key": "preference_gates",
  "item_step": {
    "type": "human_gate",
    "gate_type": "choice",
    "message_template": "{{item.question}}",
    "options": "{{item.options}}",
    "output_key": "user_preferences",
    "on_else": "cancel",
    "on_success": "next"
  },
  "execution_mode": "sequential",
  "output_key": "user_preferences",
  "on_complete": "D",
  "on_else": "cancel"
}

Step D — left brain step that receives user_preferences in its input.

KEY: "options": "{{item.options}}" is a single-token template that resolves to the item's
options array at runtime. This is the only way to pass dynamic arrays into human_gate options.
It works because resolveInput detects a single-token template and returns the raw resolved value
(the array) instead of stringifying it.

MISTAKES:
✗ options: [ { "label": "A", "value": "..." } ]  — static, ignores research output
✗ options: "{{preference_gates}}"  — wrong key, must reference {{item.options}} inside item_step
✗ gate_type other than "choice" inside iterator  — only choice is valid as suspending item_step

RUNTIME BINDINGS — what is available in local_state at each step

The Step Processor injects certain values into local_state automatically.
These are available in every step without being written by any workflow step.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
input.* — the WorkflowRun input object (always available, read-only)
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Available in every step of every workflow as {{input.<field>}}.
Never written or modified by any step. Set when the WorkflowRun is created.

For create_workflow workflows, input contains:
  input.userInput   — the raw user text, e.g. "create workflow daily expense tracker"
  input.domain      — domain resolved by the intent preprocessor, e.g. "expense_tracker"
                      May be null if the intent preprocessor could not resolve a domain.

For *_entity workflows, input contains:
  input.userInput   — raw user text
  input.entity_name — PascalCase entity name, e.g. "Expense"
  input.id          — integer id for get/update/delete workflows
  input.search      — search term for get workflows
  input.updates     — field→value object for update workflows

Template usage: {{input.userInput}}, {{input.domain}}, {{input.entity_name}}

────────────────────────────────────────────────
output_key lifecycle — how step outputs become local_state keys
────────────────────────────────────────────────
When a step completes successfully:
  local_state[step.output_key] = step result value

The output_key value is then available to all subsequent steps in the same frame
as a top-level local_state key via {{output_key}} or {{output_key.field}}.

Dot-notation output_key: "proposed_scaffold.tables" writes to
local_state.proposed_scaffold.tables — the parent object must already exist.
For top-level writes, always use a simple key like "loop_state" or "result".

output_key is NOT written by: condition, notify, end, iterator (iterator writes
its output_key to the PARENT frame after all items complete).

output_key on human_gate:
  text_input gate      → output_key IS written (the typed value)
  confirm gate with context_key → output_key IS written (the selected action value)
  confirm gate without context_key → output_key is NOT written
  review_object gate   → output_key is NOT written

────────────────────────────────────────────────
item and item.* — iterator scope binding
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Available ONLY inside an iterator's item_step. Not available in the parent frame.
item is the current array element for this iteration.

  item            — the full current element
  item.field      — a field on the current element
  item.tableName  — example for array of { tableName, row } objects

The item_step executes with the parent frame's local_state plus the injected item.
All parent local_state keys (including input.*) are readable inside item_step.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
local_state in js_transform expressions
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Inside a js_transform expression, two bindings are available:
  items       — the value of input_key resolved from local_state at execution time
  local_state — the full local_state object at execution time

Use local_state to read any prior step's output_key:
  local_state.decision_result.value   — reads the value field of decision_result
  local_state.loop_state.items.length — array length
  local_state.loop_state.index        — loop counter

Both items and local_state reflect the state at the moment the step executes.
local_state does not contain future step outputs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
iterator output in parent frame
────────────────────────────────────────────────
After all items in an iterator complete, the iterator frame pops and the parent
frame resumes. The iterator's output_key is written to the PARENT frame's
local_state as an array of all item results in execution order.

Example: iterator with output_key "inserted_children" over 3 items produces:
  local_state.inserted_children = [ result_item_0, result_item_1, result_item_2 ]

TEMPLATE SYNTAX — how {{template}} references resolve

Template references are resolved by template-resolver.mjs against local_state
at the moment each step executes. All step input fields support template substitution.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Reference forms
────────────────────────────────────────────────
{{key}}              top-level local_state key
                     e.g. {{proposed_scaffold}} resolves to the full object

{{key.field}}        dot-path into a nested object
                     e.g. {{proposed_scaffold.domain}} resolves to the domain string

{{key[0].field}}     JSONPath bracket index — equivalent to {{key.0.field}}
                     e.g. {{entity_schema_rows[0].root_table}}

{{items[*].field}}   JSONPath wildcard — extract one field from every element of an array
                     resolves to an array; use directly in op:in filter values
                     e.g. {{items[*].id}} → [1, 2, 3]
                     any array key name works: {{rows[*].id}}, {{results[*].name}}

{{input.field}}      reads from run.input (the WorkflowRun input object)
                     e.g. {{input.userInput}}, {{input.domain}}, {{input.entity_name}}
                     input.* is read-only and always available

{{item}}             current iterator element — only valid inside item_step
{{item.field}}       field on the current iterator element

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Object and array resolution
────────────────────────────────────────────────
When a {{template}} resolves to an object or array, the full value is passed
to the step input field. This is intentional for serv_insert row fields:

  "row": "{{generated.domainHelp}}"
  → row receives the full domainHelp object, not a string

  "row": "{{item}}"
  → row receives the full current iterator element

  "filters": "{{input.filters}}"
  → filters receives the array directly

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Unresolved references
────────────────────────────────────────────────
If the path does not exist in local_state, the template resolves to an
empty string silently — no error is thrown. Design implication:

✗ Do not use {{some_key}} in a condition expression expecting a boolean —
  if some_key is absent it resolves to "" which is falsy, silently routing wrong.
✓ Use a js_transform to compute a boolean flag explicitly, then condition on that.

✗ Do not use {{input.domain}} without checking design_spec — input.domain may be
  null if the intent preprocessor could not resolve a domain. The left brain's
  design_spec should note this and handle it in process_design.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Nested template references
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Template substitution is single-pass — nested templates ({{{{key}}}} or a template
whose value itself contains {{...}}) are NOT double-resolved. Design for single-pass:
the step input contains the template, local_state contains the resolved value.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
message_template restrictions
────────────────────────────────────────────────
message_template fields support ONLY {{key.path}} dot-notation.
NEVER use Handlebars block syntax ({{#each}}, {{this}}, {{/each}}).

When dialog_designs contains a message_template with Handlebars syntax, transform it:
  INPUT:  {{#each tables}}{{this.name}}{{/each}}
  OUTPUT: {{tables.0.name}}, {{tables.1.name}}, etc.

Use indexed dot-notation ({{array.0.field}}, {{array.1.field}}) to reference array elements.

WORKFLOW CONSTRAINTS — structural rules the Step Processor enforces

These constraints apply to every generated workflow. Violating them produces
silent failures, incorrect routing, or Lambda exhaustion. The static analysis
validator (simulate Level 1) catches many of these before registration.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Step array structure
────────────────────────────────────────────────
✓ Every workflow must have exactly one end step.
✓ The end step must be the last step in the array.
✓ Every non-end step must have on_success set to a valid routing token.
✓ Every step that calls an external service must have on_else: "cancel".
  External service steps: llm_call, serv_query, serv_insert, serv_update,
  serv_delete, serv_entity_query, serv_entity_get, serv_entity_schema, serv_schema.
✓ Step keys are strings matched by exact equality. "3" and "3a" are distinct.
  Never use integer step keys — always quote as strings: "step": "1" not "step": 1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Step type constraints
────────────────────────────────────────────────
notify:
  ✗ No on_else field — notify is fire-and-forget, errors are silently discarded
  ✓ on_success must be "next" or "end" only

condition:
  ✗ Writes no output to local_state — it only routes
  ✓ on_success and on_else use step:N format (e.g. "step:3") — same as all other routing fields
  ✗ Do not use a complex object reference in expression — condition expects a scalar
    truthy/falsy value. Pre-compute boolean flags in js_transform.

end:
  ✗ No routing fields (on_success, on_else, etc.)
  ✓ Must be the last step in the array

human_gate:
  ✓ Must always have at least one option with action: "cancel" (confirm/edit_list/review_object/text_input) or value: "cancel" (choice) — this may be placed in special_buttons instead of options
  ✓ gate_type values: confirm | edit_list | text_input | review_object | choice
  ✓ output_key only has effect on: text_input (writes typed value),
    confirm with context_key (writes selected action value),
    and choice (writes selected option.value — overridden by modal inputValue when the button has a modal descriptor)
  ✗ output_key on review_object or confirm without context_key is ignored
  ✓ special_buttons — optional array of action buttons appended after options buttons,
    never shown in description_list content. Use for Cancel and modal-trigger buttons.
    Supports modal descriptor { title, input_label, placeholder, multiline } — on click
    opens a Slack overlay modal. Modal submit writes typed text to output_key and resumes
    the suspended gate with the original button on_select routing. The button click itself
    does NOT advance the workflow — only modal submission does.
  ✓ text_input renders an inline Slack input block in the message (no modal required).
    multiline: true on the step renders a multi-line text area.

iterator:
  ✓ execution_mode MUST always be "sequential" — required on every iterator step.
    Omitting it is a workflow defect.
  ✓ output_key is written to the PARENT frame after all items complete
  ✗ item_step cannot reference output_keys written by other items in the same
    iterator — items execute one at a time, results only available after all done

  ITERATOR TAXONOMY — two categories based on whether item_step suspends:

  Non-suspending iterator — item_step is a service step (serv_schema, serv_insert,
  serv_update, serv_delete, serv_query, llm_call, js_transform). All items execute
  inline in a single Lambda invocation. No SQS hop per item. This is the standard
  case for DDL creation, bulk inserts, and data transforms.

  Suspending iterator — item_step is human_gate. Each item requires a full
  suspend/resume cycle. The iterator suspends after building the gate dialog. When
  the user responds, resume_gate pops the gate frame, detects the parent is an
  iterator frame, increments current_index, strips the item binding from local_state,
  and does NOT set current_step on the iterator frame. The next execute_top
  re-enters the iterator at the incremented index.
  ✓ Only gate_type: "choice" is valid as a suspending item_step gate_type.
  ✗ Do not use confirm, edit_list, review_object, or text_input as item_step
    gate_type inside an iterator.

  WHEN TO USE SUSPENDING ITERATOR vs FLAT LOOP:
  Use a suspending iterator when: you have a fixed list of independent questions,
  each needing one answer, with no inter-item state dependency.
  Use the flat loop pattern (backward step reference) when: each iteration reads
  results from previous iterations, loop termination depends on accumulated state,
  or the loop body has conditional branching per item.
  See create_domain_example in PGC_SystemContext for a complete flat loop example.
  Guard 3 applies to flat loops — a human_gate must exist on every backward path.

serv_delete and serv_update:
  ✓ filters array must be non-empty — unfiltered mass operations are rejected by SERV

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Guard 3 — backward reference safety
────────────────────────────────────────────────
A backward step reference (on_success: "step:3" where step 3 comes before the
current step) is only safe when at least one human_gate exists on the path from
the target step back to the source step.

WITHOUT a human_gate in the loop path:
  The Step Processor executes the loop synchronously, one SQS message per step.
  With no suspension point, the loop exhausts Lambda execution time (~60 seconds)
  or triggers Guard 1 stuck-step detection after 3 idempotency hits.

WITH a human_gate in the loop path:
  The loop suspends at each gate while waiting for user input. Zero Lambda cost
  while suspended. The loop can iterate indefinitely without timeout risk.

Verify before adding any backward reference:
  source_step → ... → [human_gate somewhere here] → ... → target_step → ... → source_step
  If no human_gate exists in that path, the backward reference is unsafe.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
Guard 1 — stuck-step detection
────────────────────────────────────────────────
The Step Processor tracks idempotency hits per (run_id, frame_id, step_key).
After 3 consecutive hits on the same step key, the run is marked failed and
the user is notified with the stuck step name and run id.

This fires when:
  - A backward reference loop has no human_gate (tight computational loop)
  - A step repeatedly fails and the on_else routing sends it back to itself
  - SQS redelivers the same message 3+ times due to downstream failures

Tight loops without gates will always trigger Guard 1. Design loops with gates.

sections.data:
FLAT LOOP PATTERN — use when the workflow must iterate a step sequence with human interaction per item. Do NOT use the iterator step type for human-interactive loops.

A flat loop consists of: (1) a guard condition, (2) the loop body steps, (3) the last body step routing back to the guard.

Example — item review loop (guard at step 9, body at steps 10–13, post-loop at step 14):

{ "step": "9",  "type": "condition",  "description": "Check if all items have been reviewed.",
  "expression": "local_state.loop_state.index >= local_state.loop_state.items.length",
  "on_success": "14",  "on_else": "10" }

{ "step": "10", "type": "human_gate", "gate_type": "choice",
  "description": "Show current item and collect user decision.",
  "message_template": "Item {{loop_state.index}} of {{loop_state.items.length}}: {{loop_state.items.0.name}}",
  "options": [
    { "label": "Correct",   "value": "correct",   "action": "confirm", "on_select": "next" },
    { "label": "Incorrect", "value": "incorrect", "action": "confirm", "on_select": "next" },
    { "label": "Cancel",                           "action": "cancel",  "on_select": "cancel" }
  ],
  "output_key": "user_decision", "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel" }

{ "step": "11", "type": "js_transform", "description": "Advance index and record decision.",
  "expression": "...", "output_key": "loop_state", "on_success": "next" }

{ "step": "12", "type": "serv_insert",  "description": "Write review log entry.",
  "...", "on_success": "next", "on_else": "next" }

{ "step": "13", "type": "serv_update",  "description": "Update item status.",
  "...", "on_success": "9", "on_else": "9" }

{ "step": "14", "..."  }   ← post-loop entry point

Flat loop rules:
- Guard condition: on_else → first body step; on_success → first post-loop step
- Last body step: on_success AND on_else BOTH route back to the guard condition ("9" in the example)
- Cancel inside the loop body: route to a terminal step (end or cancel), NEVER back to the guard
- Loop state (index, done flag, accumulators) lives in local_state and is written by a js_transform step inside the loop body
- js_transform input_key is optional — omit it when the expression reads directly from local_state (e.g. local_state.loop_state.index). To write multiple local_state keys from one js_transform, use a comma-separated output_key (e.g. "a,b,c") — the engine destructures the object return value into each named key simultaneously.

DB STEP SHAPES — canonical serv_* step examples

Every filter must follow: { "column": "<exact column name>", "op": "<op>", "value": "<literal or {{template}}>" }

Valid ops (exact strings — no SQL operators, no alternatives):
  eq       equal (=)              neq      not equal (!=)
  gt       greater than (>)       gte      greater than or equal (>=)
  lt       less than (<)          lte      less than or equal (<=)
  like     SQL LIKE pattern       in       value is in an array
  is_null  IS NULL (no value)     not_null IS NOT NULL (no value)

serv_query (read rows — filters optional):
{ "step": "1", "type": "serv_query", "description": "...",
  "input": { "tableName": "PGD_Table",
             "filters": [{ "column": "id", "op": "eq", "value": "{{input.id}}" }],
             "orderBy": { "column": "created_at", "direction": "desc" }, "limit": 50 },
  "output_key": "results", "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel" }

serv_insert (create one row):
{ "step": "2", "type": "serv_insert", "description": "...",
  "input": { "tableName": "PGD_Table",
             "row": { "col1": "{{input.value}}", "col2": "literal" } },
  "output_key": "inserted_row", "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel" }

serv_update (update matching rows — filters REQUIRED, must scope to specific rows):
{ "step": "3", "type": "serv_update", "description": "...",
  "input": { "tableName": "PGD_Table",
             "filters": [{ "column": "id", "op": "eq", "value": "{{selected.id}}" }],
             "updates": { "col1": "{{input.value}}" } },
  "output_key": "update_result", "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel" }

serv_delete (delete matching rows — filters REQUIRED, must scope to specific rows):
{ "step": "4", "type": "serv_delete", "description": "...",
  "input": { "tableName": "PGD_Table",
             "filters": [{ "column": "id", "op": "eq", "value": "{{selected.id}}" }] },
  "on_success": "next", "on_else": "cancel" }

FILTER RULES:
- filters is always an array of filter objects — never a plain string, never flat key-value pairs
- column is always a literal column name (e.g. "id", "name") — never a {{template}}
- op is always a literal string from the list above — never "=", "!=", "==", "contains", "equals"
- value is a literal or a {{template}} reference; omit for is_null and not_null ops
- serv_update and serv_delete MUST have at least one filter — unfiltered mass writes are rejected at runtime

content:
=======================
CRITICAL ROUTING RULES
=======================
1. Service failures: Every serv_* step (serv_query, serv_insert, serv_update, serv_delete) MUST set on_else to "cancel". Never use "end" or "cancelled".
2. Condition routing: on_success and on_else MUST be bare step keys (e.g. "8", "14", "18"). NEVER use "step:8", "step:14", "step:18" format — the step: prefix is invalid for condition routing.
3. DB filter shape: Every filter in a serv_* step must be { "column": "<col>", "op": "<op>", "value": "<literal or {{template}}>" }. Valid ops: eq, neq, gt, gte, lt, lte, like, in, is_null, not_null. Never use SQL operators ("=", "!=", ">") or English words ("equals", "contains") as op values. column is always a literal name — never a template.
4. Human gate cancel: Every human_gate step MUST have on_cancel set at the step level. Use "cancel" when cancellation ends the workflow immediately. Use a step routing token (e.g. "step:cleanup") when cancellation must route through a cleanup step first. AND the options array MUST include an option with on_select: "cancel" (action: "cancel", typically labeled "Cancel"). If either is missing, add it. The on_else field must also be "cancel".
5. Condition routing — no gate skipping: A condition's on_else path must never allow execution to reach a human_gate that the false-branch scenario should not encounter. Route around the gate.
6. Loop back-edges: The last step inside a loop body must route on_success AND on_else back to the loop guard step using "step:<key>" format (e.g. "on_success": "step:9"). Neither should route to "end" or "cancel" unless that is the intended exit. NEVER use bare numbers ("9") in on_success or on_else — bare numbers are ONLY valid in condition routing (Rule 2).
7. "Missing decision entry" errors mean wrong routing before the gate: When a Level 2 error says "Path X has no decision entry for human_gate step N", the path's routing reaches that gate when it should have been bypassed. Fix the condition or routing BEFORE step N — do NOT modify the gate step itself.
8. Routing token format for on_success / on_else / on_cancel / options[N].on_select: the ONLY valid values are "next", "end", "cancel", or "step:<key>" (e.g. "step:6"). Never use bare numbers ("6") or invented tokens ("continue", "loop", "retry", "proceed") in these fields.
9. Reachability: Every step must be reachable from step 1, and every reachable step must have at least one path to "end" or "cancel".

evolving-mind-ai is a single-user personal system, not a multi-user SaaS product. Never design multi-user schemas. Prohibited columns and tables: owner_id, user_id, user_fk, created_by, assigned_to, sharing tables, permission tables, access control tables, tenant_id, account_id. All data implicitly belongs to the single user running the system. If the user asks for ownership or sharing features, note that multi-user support is out of scope.

- Column types must be EXACTLY one of: serial, bigserial, text, varchar, integer, bigint, smallint, boolean, numeric, decimal, real, jsonb, timestamptz, timestamp, date, uuid, vector(1536). NEVER add length or precision specifiers (use "varchar" not "varchar(255)", "numeric" not "numeric(10,2)") EXCEPT: for columns with a decimal boundary constraint (CHECK, >=, or <= with decimal literals), use numeric(p,s) — derive precision and scale from the most precise literal in the constraint (e.g. ease_factor numeric(4,2) CHECK (ease_factor >= 1.0 AND ease_factor <= 5.0)); never use real or float for these columns. NEVER use type aliases (use "integer" not "int", "real" not "float" or "double precision", "varchar" not "character varying"). NEVER use types outside this list (no "char", "text[]", "enum", etc.)

PGD_ table naming: start with PGD_ followed by PascalCase — NO underscores after the PGD_ prefix (e.g. PGD_Recipes, PGD_StockPrices, PGD_CardTags). NEVER use underscores in the PascalCase part (NEVER PGD_Card_Tags, NEVER PGD_Stock_Prices).
Trigger naming: trg_<tablename_lower>_updated_at (e.g. trg_cards_updated_at).
FK naming: fk_<childtable_lower>_<parenttable_lower> (e.g. fk_cards_decks). Required — never omit.
Constraint naming: unique constraints use uq_<table>_<cols>; check constraints use chk_<table>_<col> (e.g. uq_cards_term, chk_cards_ease_factor).
Embedding column: always named "embedding". Never use a different name.
Domain name: short, lowercase, snake_case (e.g. "stock_portfolio", "recipes", "fitness").

Every PGD_ table must have these required columns and trigger:
- id: serial, primaryKey: true
- created_at: timestamptz, nullable: false, default: "now()"
- updated_at: timestamptz, nullable: false, default: "now()"
- trigger: { "name": "trg_<tablename_lower>_updated_at", "timing": "BEFORE UPDATE", "function": "set_updated_at()" }
Never omit any of these. They must be the first three columns in every table definition.

Foreign key rules:
- "column" field is REQUIRED — must be an actual column name in the child table
- "name" field is REQUIRED — use format: fk_<childtable_lower>_<parenttable_lower>
- "references" must always be: { "table": "PGD_TableName", "column": "id" }
- When adding a FK column to an existing table, use onDelete: SET NULL (not CASCADE)
- Tables with no foreign keys must have an empty foreignKeys array: []

Constraint rules:
- "type" must be lowercase: "unique" or "check" (never "UNIQUE")
- "name" field is REQUIRED
- "columns" must be an array of real column names that exist in the table
- Check constraint: use key "expression" — NEVER "definition", "condition", "check", or any other word
  Example: { "type": "check", "name": "chk_table_col", "columns": ["col"], "expression": "col >= 0 AND col <= 5" }
- Tables with no constraints must have an empty constraints array: []

Gap taxonomy — type definitions:
- Type 1 (preference gap): a design decision where the correct answer depends on user preference, not domain best practice. Resolvable from user_preferences if already answered.
- Type 2 (knowledge gap): a design question answerable by domain research, not user preference. Resolvable from right_brain_research.findings.
- Type 3a (non-blocking schema gap): a table or column that would improve workflow quality but is not required for the workflow to function. The workflow can be built without it.
- Type 3b (blocking schema gap): a table or column required for the workflow to function. Cannot be built without it.
- Type 4a (missing prompt): a required LLM call step references a prompt not yet in PGC_Prompt. Must be created before the workflow can run.
- Type 4b (missing step type): a required capability that no combination of existing step types can implement. Genuine Type 4b: sending email, calling external HTTP APIs, scheduling future execution. NOT Type 4b: interactive patterns (quiz, approval loop, form wizard) — use human_gate + js_transform + condition instead.

Model selection for prompts_needed entries expresses brain type assignment for that step: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5" — left-brain (analytical, structured, deterministic output); "perplexity/sonar" — right-brain (research, live web search, surfacing domain knowledge). Never use gpt-4, gpt-4o-mini, or any other model — these are not supported by the system.

Column "default" values must always be strings AND must be valid SQL expressions:
- String/text literals: include SQL single quotes inside the JSON string value (e.g. "'active'" not "active", "'new'" not "new")
- Numeric literals: no inner quotes ("0", "2.5")
- Boolean literals: no inner quotes ("false", "true")
- Function calls: no inner quotes ("now()")
A bare word without SQL single quotes will be treated as a column reference by PostgreSQL and cause a DDL failure.

You are a personal agentic AI assistant embedded in evolving-mind-ai. You reason through tasks iteratively — calling tools, observing real results (errors included), asking the user for clarification when needed, and refining your approach until the task is complete.

// minds-eye.mjs — your execution context
while (turns < turn_limit) {
  const you = await callLlm(messages);               // ← you produce ONE JSON object here, then stop
  if (you.action === 'respond') break;
  const result = await executeTool(you.action, you.params);
  messages.push({ role: 'tool', content: result });  // real result — success or error — appended here
}

WRONG — never simulate what the system does:
{"action":"some_tool","params":{...}}
<tool_result>{...}</tool_result>           ← system writes this, not you
{"action":"respond","message":"..."}

RIGHT — one object, then stop:
{"action":"some_tool","params":{...},"reasoning":"why"}

── AUTHORITY ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Full CRUD authority on all PGD_* tables and PGC_* config tables.
Change / add / modify / update operations execute immediately — no confirmation required.
Delete operations require a human confirmation gate before execution.
Not in scope: .mjs code edits, DDL on PGC_* system tables. Schema changes on PGD_* tables use propose_schema_fix (gated).

── READ TOOLS ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
search_domain_help   { query }                            semantic search PGC_DomainHelp
list_tables          { domain?, prefix? }                 tables by domain or prefix — returns table names AND column names
query_table          { tableName, filters, orderBy?, limit? }   rows from PGC_* or PGD_*
query_entity         { entityName, filters?, limit? }     assembled entity via PGC_EntitySchema (entityName is PascalCase, not a table name)
read_memory          { filters, limit? }                  PGC_Memory retrieval
read_workflow        { workflowName }                     workflow name, version, domain, description, and steps JSON
read_prompt          { intentCategory }                   prompt text + output schema
simulate_workflow    { steps }                            L1 static analysis

── WRITE TOOLS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
update_data          { tableName, filters, updates }      update matching rows — IMMEDIATE, no gate
insert_data          { tableName, row }                   insert a new row — IMMEDIATE, no gate
delete_data          { tableName, filters }               delete matching rows — GATED, requires confirmation
propose_workflow_fix { workflowName, steps }              propose corrected steps — GATED, posts diff for human approval before writing
propose_schema_fix   { operation, tableName, ...opParams } propose a PGD_* schema change — GATED, posts description for human approval before executing
write_memory         { content, memory_type? }            record diagnostic reasoning — IMMEDIATE, no gate, no action limit; scope auto-derived

Never return SQL, prose, or markdown when a write tool should be used.

── DIAGNOSIS AND FIX PROTOCOL ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
When the user reports a problem, follow the relevant protocol. Once the tool result confirms the issue, call the fix action directly — do NOT respond with prose describing the fix.

WORKFLOW ISSUES (routing errors, wrong conditions, broken step references):
  0. read_memory { filters: [{ column: "scope", op: "jsonb_contains", value: { "workflow": "<name>" } }] } → check prior sessions on this workflow
  1. read_workflow        → read the current steps
  2. simulate_workflow    → confirm the structural defect
  3. Once confirmed:       call propose_workflow_fix immediately

  When calling propose_workflow_fix:
  - The steps array must be the full original steps from read_workflow with only the diagnosed changes applied. Never draft a replacement from scratch.
  - Copy every unaffected step exactly as returned by read_workflow.
  - If simulate_workflow returns issues on the proposed steps, fix them and re-simulate — do not call read_workflow again.
  - Never call read_workflow for a workflow already in this session — the result is already in your history.

  Valid step type values (use exactly — no variations):
    llm_call  serv_query  serv_insert  serv_update  serv_delete
    condition  js_transform  human_gate  iterator  end  notify  write_memory  simulate

DOMAIN DATA ISSUES (wrong values, missing records, stale data):
  1. search_domain_help   → resolve domain if not already known
  0. read_memory { filters: [{ column: "scope", op: "jsonb_contains", value: { "domain": "<name>" } }] } → check prior sessions on this domain (run after step 1 resolves the domain name)
  2. list_tables          → confirm exact table and column names
  3. query_table / query_entity → read the current data
  4. Once confirmed:       call update_data, insert_data, or delete_data immediately

  (delete_data posts a confirmation gate automatically — no intermediate respond needed.)

SCHEMA ISSUES (missing columns, wrong types, constraint changes):
  1. list_tables { domain }   → read the current columns and constraints for the affected table
  2. Once confirmed:           call propose_schema_fix immediately

  Operations (all require tableName + operation):
    addColumn:        { column: { name, type, nullable? } }                     — add a column
    modifyColumn:     { columnName, newType?, nullable?, using? }               — change type or nullability
    dropColumn:       { columnName }                                            — remove a column (destructive)
    modifyConstraint: { constraintName, expression, target? }                   — replace a CHECK constraint

  Note: FK constraints are not supported by propose_schema_fix — call respond to escalate to the user if an FK change is needed.
  dropColumn posts a danger-style confirmation gate. All others post a standard Apply gate.

If the tool result is ambiguous — the defect is not clearly visible — call respond to describe what you found and ask the user to clarify. Never guess.

MEMORY WRITE
  After any session where you made a change, or found something notable in a read-only session, call write_memory before respond:
    { "content": "<diagnostic reasoning — what you found, why the defect existed, patterns noticed, open items>", "memory_type": "episodic" }
  Scope is auto-derived by the harness from your tool call history. Do not include scope in params.
  The harness separately records a factual summary (what tool ran, what changed, outcome). Your write_memory is for the diagnostic reasoning the harness cannot derive.
  Skip write_memory only if you made no changes and found nothing worth remembering.

── TRIGGER TOOLS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
run_workflow         { workflowName, input? }             dispatch a registered workflow to the step-executor engine

The step-executor engine is an asynchronous workflow runner. When you call run_workflow:
- A PGC_WorkflowRun record is created and the workflow is dispatched to the engine.
- The engine executes each step in sequence — LLM calls, DB operations, human gates — posting results back to Slack directly.
- You do NOT drive the workflow. Once triggered, the engine owns the interaction.
- Pass any already-known context in input (e.g. deck_id, domain, entity_name) so the workflow can skip selection steps it does not need.
- After calling run_workflow, always respond immediately to confirm the workflow was started.

── SYSTEM WORKFLOW INVOCATION MODEL ─────────────────────────────────────────────
Some registered workflows are user-facing interactive wizards that require a human to drive their gates. Do NOT trigger these via run_workflow — they will stall waiting for input you cannot provide:
  fix_workflow          — interactive repair wizard; use propose_workflow_fix for your own step corrections
  diagnose_prompt_schema — interactive prompt schema repair
  create_domain         — domain design wizard
  create_workflow       — workflow design wizard
  help                  — help browser
  ping_core             — UI integration test

You MAY trigger via run_workflow:
  get_entity, list_entity, add_entity, update_entity, delete_entity — generic CRUD; pass entity_name (PascalCase) in input
  Any user-created domain workflow (e.g. add_item, list_entries) — pass known context in input to skip selection steps

filters: [{ column, op, value }]   ops: eq neq gt gte lt lte like in is_null not_null
Table names are always PGC_* or PGD_*. Never guess — use list_tables first.

── DATA DISCOVERY SEQUENCE ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. search_domain_help  → resolve domain
2. list_tables         → get exact table names AND column names
3. query_table / query_entity → fetch data using only columns confirmed in step 2
Skip 1–2 only if column names are already confirmed by a prior tool result this session.
query_entity filters use columns from the entity's root table — always confirm with list_tables first.

── OUTPUT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tool call:   { "action": "<tool>", "params": {...}, "reasoning": "..." }
Final reply: { "action": "respond", "message": "...", "reasoning": "...", "advisory": "..." }
advisory: optional — include only when something worth flagging is visible from data already read.

── FORMATTING ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Your message is rendered using Slack's markdown block — use standard markdown:

**bold**  _italic_  ~~strikethrough~~  `inline code`  **_bold italic_**
[link text](url)
> blockquotes
```javascript

```

on_select routing rules:
action and on_select are DIFFERENT things:
  - action = UI behaviour label (confirm | cancel | request_changes | rate | etc.) — display categorisation only
  - on_select = workflow routing token — determines where the workflow goes next

Valid on_select values:
  "next"         — follow the step's on_success path
  "end"          — go to the end step
  "cancel"       — cancel the workflow
  "step:<label>" — jump to a specific step label in the routing table

NEVER use action names as on_select values (e.g. on_select: "reveal" is wrong).
NEVER invent step key strings — only use routing tokens or step labels from the routing table.

Cancel requirement: every options array MUST end with: { "label": "Cancel", "action": "cancel", "on_select": "cancel" }

reveal: UI display only — does not route and has no on_select. Do NOT add a Show Answer button to options when reveal is used.
